stem: During living kidney donor informed consent, what must the donor commit to regarding post-donation follow-up?

options.text: Postoperative follow-up testing coordinated by the live donor program
No follow-up visits after hospital discharge
Follow-up only if the recipient develops rejection
Lifetime immunosuppression monitoring at the recipient's transplant center only

explanation.rationale_correct: Living donor education and consent require the donor to commit to postoperative follow-up testing coordinated by the live donor program, with OPTN living-donor follow-up reporting responsibilities.

rationale_incorrect.B: Donors must commit to structured postoperative follow-up, not discharge without monitoring.
rationale_incorrect.C: Donor follow-up is required regardless of recipient outcomes.
rationale_incorrect.D: Donor follow-up is coordinated by the live donor program; it is not the same as recipient immunosuppression monitoring.

primary_anchor.section: Ch. 7, Living Donation → F. Informed Consent → 6.
primary_anchor.quote_hint: donor must commit to postoperative follow-up testing coordinated by the live donor program

references.citation: Core Curriculum for Transplant Nurses, 2nd ed. (Cupples et al., 2016).
references.locator: Ch. 7 → F. Elements Included in Education and Informed Consent → 6. (postoperative follow-up testing commitment); PDF p. 340 (repo file-page index; printed margin may differ).

notes: Source-first item. Fifth 010700 item; distinct from discharge fever call (cctc-1026); anchor verified on Cupples p. 340.

stem: A living liver donor without a surgical drain develops right shoulder pain, chills, and fever on postoperative day 4. Which complication should the coordinator include in donor teaching as a possible explanation?

options.text: Bile leak from the cut liver surface
Expected normal healing that never requires evaluation
Mandatory graft nephrectomy in the donor

explanation.rationale_correct: When no drain is placed after living liver donation, right shoulder pain, chills, fever, and elevated white blood cell count may indicate a bile leak from the cut liver surface.

rationale_incorrect.B: These symptoms warrant evaluation and may indicate a bile leak rather than assumed benign healing.
rationale_incorrect.C: Recipient rejection is not the donor complication described for shoulder pain and fever after liver donation.
rationale_incorrect.D: Bile leak monitoring is the concern; nephrectomy does not apply to liver donors.

primary_anchor.section: Ch. 7, Living Donation → postoperative monitoring → f.iii.
primary_anchor.quote_hint: right shoulder pain, chills, fever … could indicate a bile leak

stem: When teaching transplant candidates about immunosuppressive medication risks, which side effect should be included in standard education?

options.text: Permanent elimination of all infection risk
Guaranteed weight loss without dietary change

explanation.rationale_correct: Transplant risk education includes common immunosuppressive and antimicrobial medication side effects such as hyperglycemia, hypertension, kidney dysfunction, and digestive problems.

rationale_incorrect.B: Immunosuppression increases infection risk rather than eliminating it.
rationale_incorrect.C: Weight gain, not guaranteed weight loss, is among described medication side effects.
rationale_incorrect.D: Immunosuppression is associated with infection and malignancy risks, not cancer immunity.

primary_anchor.section: Ch. 3, Patient Education → §6. Risks → g. Medication side effects → ii.

references.citation: Core Curriculum for Transplant Nurses, 2nd ed. (Cupples et al., 2016).
references.locator: Ch. 3 → §6. Risks → g. Medication side effects → ii. (common side effects taught to patients); PDF p. 100 (repo file-page index; printed margin may differ).

stem: A coordinator is updating discharge medication teaching for kidney recipients. Evaluate the following statements:

elements.text: Grapefruit may increase serum levels of certain immunosuppression medications.
Recipients should notify the transplant team before starting any new medication prescribed by another provider.
Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs may be used freely without renal risk after transplant.
A written medication roster with times and doses supports accurate home dosing.

explanation.rationale_correct: Medication teaching includes grapefruit interactions, notifying the transplant team before new prescriptions, avoiding nonsteroidal medications because of renal toxicity risk, and using a written roster with dosing times.

rationale_incorrect.A: Statement IV is also correct—a written medication roster supports adherence.
rationale_incorrect.C: Statement III is false; recipients should avoid nonsteroidal medications unless approved because of renal toxicity risk.
rationale_incorrect.D: Statement III is false; not all four statements are correct.

primary_anchor.section: Ch. 3, Patient Education → medication management (Right way / Other)
primary_anchor.quote_hint: grapefruit … increase serum levels … notify the transplant team … avoid non-steroidal medications

references.citation: Core Curriculum for Transplant Nurses, 2nd ed. (Cupples et al., 2016).
references.locator: Ch. 3 → medication management → Right way (grapefruit interactions, food/drug interactions) and Other (notify team, avoid NSAIDs, written roster); PDF p. 108 (repo file-page index; printed margin may differ).
